title: The big lookout
hook: year one is done; ahead lie the ranges: the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru, the Granth itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, sarbat: every Ardas ends by asking good for everyone, and your line, for everyone, not just us. Today, the lookout.

Near the top of a long hike, tired legs earn a stop. A hiker turns around, and there it is: the whole valley walked through, small and golden below. Then the other way: more mountains, bigger ones, blue in the distance. Two thoughts can arrive at once: I made it, and look how much more there is. This is that spot, the last day of year one.
screen: `A TIRED HIKER TURNS AROUND.` → `THE VALLEY BEHIND, SMALL AND GOLDEN.` → `MORE MOUNTAINS AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the word Sikh. It's usually traced to an old Indian word for a student, a disciple, a learner. Sikhs often put it simply: a Sikh is someone who keeps learning from the Guru, not someone who finishes. So a year doesn't end with a diploma; it ends at a lookout. Turn around first. You began with first words: seva, Waheguru, Ik Onkar, langar, sangat. Then the stories: ten Gurus, one light. Then the practices: kirtan, simran, Nitnem, a visit to the gurdwara. Then the Japji, pauri by pauri, all thirty-eight and the saloks. Then the depths: the Granth's great themes, Kabir and Farid, the rehat, the history, and the grief of 1984 carried carefully. That's the valley. Now face the other way. Four ranges. First, the daily banis: Jaap Sahib tomorrow, then Anand Sahib, Rehras, Kirtan Sohila, Sukhmani, the prayers many Sikhs say morning and evening. Then Sikh history, told slowly, century by century. Then the ways of the Guru, lived day to day. And then the Granth itself, fourteen hundred thirty pages, the Guru Sikhs bow to. Daunting? Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit to meet it with, from day seventeen: chardi kala. Rising spirits, an unbeaten, upward-facing mind. It sits in the Ardas's last line, right beside yesterday's good of all. Chardi kala isn't pretending things are easy. The Sikh story has plenty of hard days, and this year's path passed through some of them. It's facing forward anyway, in good heart, because the road is long and the company is good. That's the lookout: grateful behind, awake ahead.
screen: `SIKH: A LEARNER WHO KEEPS LEARNING.` · `THE VALLEY: WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, DEPTHS.` · `THE RANGES: BANIS, STORY, WAYS, GRANTH.` · `CHARDI KALA: FACE FORWARD, IN GOOD HEART.` · then, large: `WOW.`

segments.voice: Find a window and let your eyes go as far as they can: a rooftop, a tree, a strip of sky. Breathe slowly and think back over one word, one story, one practice that stayed with you this year; then let your gaze go to the edge of what you can see, and notice there is more out there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru under your breath, the Sikh word of wonder from camp one; if not, simply stay with what you see.
Chardi kala. Rising spirits, an unbeaten, upward-facing mind — the spirit to meet the ranges ahead, the banis and the Granth, at the top of year one.
Your line: wow. For a sky, a kindness, a sentence that lands. Year one, done.

screen: `DAY 331 COUNTS.` → `YEAR ONE, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: THE TENTH GURU'S MORNING PRAISE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs often describe themselves as lifelong learners of the Guru, and the Ardas said at the close of gurdwara gatherings ends by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and the good of all.

fork.setup: you've climbed a whole year of the path and reached the lookout. what does the word Sikh suggest comes next?
options: stop here: the learning is complete.
keep walking: a Sikh is a learner for life.
go back to the bottom and start over.
fork.reveal: the word Sikh is usually traced to a word for a learner or disciple. the lookout isn't the end of the road; ahead lie the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru and the Granth itself.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chardi kala, rising spirits; the mood Sikhs meet the road ahead with, named in the Ardas's last line.

trapdoor: what you thought: a year of lessons ends at a finish line.
what it means: it ends at a lookout, grateful for the valley behind and awake to the ranges ahead, in chardi kala.
what a scholar hears: Sikh is usually traced to Sanskrit shishya, disciple (compare Pali sikkha, training); Sikhs read the name as a learner for life.
recall: singing the Guru's hymns in praise of God

chat.says: You finished a whole year. Are you done learning about Sikhi now?
options: No, a Sikh is a learner; the year ends at a lookout, facing forward.
Yes, one year covers it all, so there's nothing left to study.
Only scholars keep learning; everyone else stops after the basics.
chat.meaning: Sikh is traced to an old word for a learner. Chardi kala faces the long road ahead in good heart: grateful behind, awake ahead.

notes: Year one close. The look-back list (first words, stories, practices, Japji, depths including 1984) summarizes camps 1–5; confirm it fairly represents the year.
Etymology of 'Sikh' from Sanskrit shishya (disciple), with Pali sikkha as a related form: confirm wording.
Chardi kala is placed in the last line of the Ardas beside sarbat da bhala; Gurmukhi ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ and pronunciation CHUR-dee KA-laa to be checked.

The four ranges ahead (daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru, the Granth itself) follow the outline for years two to five; the year-two bani list (Jaap Sahib, Anand Sahib, Rehras, Kirtan Sohila, Sukhmani) follows y2.md.
Chardi kala was camp one's word on day fifteen; the teach refers back to it.
